Graph-RAG and Graph-Augmented Agents.
Graph-RAG systems Edge et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025b) extend retrieval to knowledge graphs, enabling multi-hop reasoning and improved coverage over large corpora. Recent work explores optimizing the interface between knowledge graphs and LLMs Marković et al. (2025) ; Coppolillo (2025) and integrating knowledge graph reasoning into agent workflows Besta et al. (2025) . GraphRAG Edge et al. (2024) constructs entity knowledge graphs, partitions them into community hierarchies, and pre-generates summaries aggregated at query time. Think-on-Graph Sun et al. (2024) performs iterative reasoning by exploring knowledge graph relations, while Reasoning on Graphs Luo et al. (2024) generates faithful reasoning plans grounded in graph structure. Theorem-of-Thought Abdaljalil et al. (2025) runs three specialized agents in parallel, stores each agent’s step-wise reasoning as a graph, and then applies Bayesian belief propagation to score these graphs and select the most coherent one. StructGPT Jiang et al. (2023) provides a general framework for reasoning over structured data. However, their inference semantics are append-only : evidence is accumulated globally, with no explicit hypothesis representation, revision trigger, or localized propagation operator. This makes them order-sensitive and brittle under evolving evidence, especially when graphs are large and cannot be fully materialized in context.
Diagnostic Agents in Operations.
LLM agents for diagnosis in cloud operations span several architectures: tool-assisted RCA agents Roy et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Deshpande et al. (2025) , multi-agent systems like STRATUS Chen et al. (2025) , and graph-augmented workflows like GALA Tian et al. (2025) . Recent work also provides systematic taxonomies of failure modes in such diagnostic agents Ma et al. (2025) . These systems are explicitly abductive: they generate explanatory hypotheses from partial evidence. Graph-based systems like Groot Wang et al. (2021) and causal approaches like RADICE Tonon et al. (2025) use service dependency graphs to localize faults; similar approaches have been applied to microservice systems Zhu et al. (2024) and IoT environments with dynamic causal graphs Tang et al. (2025) . GraphLocator Liu et al. (2025a) -style traversal is captured by our Deterministic Controller’s graph-guided expansion, and GALA/SynergyRCA-style Xiang et al. (2025) evidence aggregation is subsumed by the Context Packet; neither exposes explicit belief revision or localized message passing. Nevertheless, all these systems rely on implicit hypotheses, global summarization, and workflow control rather than controller-enforced invariants over mutable graph state. Even graph-aware workflows remain monotonic, without first-class revision semantics or message passing that localizes updates to affected neighborhoods. Our ReAct baseline subsumes the inference semantics of these approaches: it has access to all diagnostic tools (topology queries, log/metric analysis, trace inspection) plus shell utilities and code execution, strictly more capability than published RCA agents. Yet even the best-performing ReAct configuration (Gemini 3 Flash) achieves only 74% majority@3 F1 on ITBench, compared to 92% for EoG with the same model. This 18-point gap persists across model families, confirming that gains arise from state semantics (explicit beliefs, revision, propagation), not domain engineering or tool access.
Causal Inference.
Causal discovery and effect estimation Wan et al. (2024) ; Vowels et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2021) target different outputs (DAGs, treatment effects) under static, fully-observed data; they do not model revisable explanatory hypotheses under streaming partial evidence and are thus not comparable to abductive graph reasoning for baseline consideration.
Putting EoG in perspective.
Our contribution is an inference abstraction for abductive reasoning under streaming evidence and unbounded graphs, where global context is infeasible and explanations must be revised online. The baselines above cover the strongest LLM instantiations of investigative reasoning; differences arise from state semantics , not domain or prompting. Table 5 summarizes the comparison across inference-semantic axes. We compare against representative ReAct, Graph-RAG, and diagnostic agents, and ablate revision and propagation—demonstrating that gains arise from state semantics rather than domain-specific engineering.
7 Conclusion
We framed operational diagnosis as abductive inference over graphs and introduced Semantic Belief Propagation, which separates local LLM reasoning from deterministic control to enable non-monotonic belief revision. Experiments on ITBench show gains in accuracy, stability, and token efficiency over ReAct-style agents. This architecture yields reproducible, auditable explanations under realistic production constraints.

Codex CLI implements a disaggregated architecture where the LLM reasoning loop is separated from tool execution OpenAI (2025) . The core is written in Rust ( codex-rs ) and provides:
•
Sandboxed Execution : Shell and code execution occur in isolated subprocesses with configurable permission levels (read-only, write workspace, full access). The sandbox restricts filesystem writes, network access, and system modifications by default.
•
MCP Tool Servers : Tools run as separate processes communicating via the Model Context Protocol. This separation enables: (1) crash isolation—a failing tool does not crash the agent; (2) resource limits—each tool server can be independently constrained; (3) extensibility—domain tools are added without modifying the core.
•
Automatic Context Summarization : When tool outputs exceed context limits, Codex summarizes content to preserve important information while staying within token bounds.
•
State Persistence : Python execution maintains state across invocations; file operations are transactional within the workspace.
A.2 ReAct Agent Prompt
The ReAct baseline operates as a Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) support agent designed for offline incident analysis. The agent follows a structured investigation workflow with explicit phases for context discovery, symptom analysis, hypothesis generation, evidence collection, and causal chain construction. The full system prompt is provided below, with environment variables ( $SNAPSHOT_DIRS , $WORKSPACE_DIR ) populated at runtime.
ReAct with Code System Prompt
Task: You are an expert SRE (Site Reliability Engineer) and Kubernetes SRE Support Agent investigating a production incident from OFFLINE snapshot data.
You are a highly capable tool-using agent able to: Diagnose Kubernetes failures; Correlate alerts, events, traces, and metrics; Identify contributing factors (not just root cause); Perform data analysis using Python when useful.
INCIDENT SNAPSHOT DATA LOCATION
Your incident data is located in $SNAPSHOT_DIRS (READ-ONLY). Do NOT search the filesystem for additional data. Start by listing the contents of these directories. Working directory: $WORKSPACE_DIR . Application topology available at $WORKSPACE_DIR/app.json .
FINAL OUTPUT FORMAT (MANDATORY)
Generate a JSON diagnosis identifying all Kubernetes entities: entities that CAUSED the incident ( contributing_factor=true ), entities IMPACTED but did not cause it ( contributing_factor=false ), and the propagation chain showing how the incident spread. Requirements: explain all firing alerts, provide reasoning/evidence for every entity, construct fault propagation chain, use Python for data analysis when necessary. Write diagnosis to $WORKSPACE_DIR/agent_output.json . Validate JSON using jq after writing.
ENTITY NAMING CONVENTION
All entities MUST use format: namespace/Kind/name . Examples: otel-demo/Deployment/ad , otel-demo/Service/frontend . Do NOT include UIDs.
PROPAGATION CHAIN (MANDATORY)
Construct chain: Root Cause → \to Intermediate Services → \to Impacted Services. Each link includes: source (causing entity), target (affected entity), condition (what state caused propagation), effect (observable effect on target).
RULES FOR CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
contributing_factor=true (IRREDUCIBLE): Mark ONLY if entity is an independent cause not fully explained by another contributing factor. Use “irreducibility test”: if failure is explained by “upstream X failed” with propagation edge X → X\to entity, then entity is NOT irreducible → \to set false .
contributing_factor=false (DERIVED): Mark entities that are downstream effects/symptoms caused by another contributing factor.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT mark both cause and derived symptom as true . Multiple contributing_factors allowed ONLY if truly independent.
DEBUGGING PRINCIPLES
(1) Differential Observability: Compare replicas and time windows.
(2) Occam’s Razor: Choose simplest explanation consistent with evidence.
(3) Duration Matching: Theory must explain entire incident duration.
(4) Follow Breadcrumbs: Let alerts/errors guide investigation.
(5) No Jumping to Conclusions: Validate every hypothesis with evidence.
(6) Chaos Files ≠ \neq Active Chaos: Verify experiment was running AND time-aligned.
(7) Semantic Name Normalization: Try variations, strip suffixes, search partial matches.
INVESTIGATION WORKFLOW (DO NOT SKIP)
Phase 1 – Context Discovery: List available files; read topology.md to understand dependencies.
Phase 2 – Symptom Analysis: Read all alert files; compute start/end time, duration, frequency; build Alerts Table.
Phase 3 – Hypothesis Generation: Create initial hypotheses; create validation plan for each.
Phase 4 – Evidence Collection Loop: Use tools and Python to gather log/event/metrics/trace evidence; validate/refute hypotheses; explain firing alerts.
Phase 5 – Causal Chain Construction: Build chain: [Config Error] → \to [CrashLoop] → \to [Service Down] → \to [Frontend 5xx].
Phase 6 – Conclusion: Ensure all alerts explained, all entities included, contributions correctly labeled; output final JSON.
PYTHON ANALYSIS (ENCOURAGED)
Write Python snippets to: parse alerts/events/metrics/traces, join datasets by timestamp or UID, extract failing spans, compute metrics deltas, identify patterns (CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, 5xx spikes). Persist snippets in Python files.
PROHIBITED ACTIONS
NEVER read ground_truth.yaml; NEVER output anything other than final JSON; NEVER hallucinate K8s objects; NEVER leave alerts unexplained.

B.2 Event-Driven Architecture
The implementation realizes the ActiveSet abstraction from § 4.3 as an event-driven message queue. This architectural choice enables concurrent node evaluation without changing the algorithm’s semantics—each event type corresponds directly to operations in the abstract algorithm.
Table 7: Event Types and Semantics
Event
Semantics
Activate(v, reason)
Evaluate node v v ; equivalent to ActiveSet.pop(v)
Message(u, v, B u B_{u} , t)
Deliver belief B u B_{u} to v v ’s inbox
BeliefChanged(v)
Broadcast B v B_{v} to neighbors; triggers re-activation
The event queue processes Activate events by: (1) checking visit eligibility, (2) collecting inbox messages, (3) fetching local context, (4) invoking the abductive policy, (5) applying damping if oscillating, (6) emitting BeliefChanged if belief changed, and (7) emitting Activate for discovered or proposed nodes. This is semantically equivalent to the ActiveSet-based loop but enables the actor model for concurrent processing.
B.3 Termination Safeguards
Beyond the damping heuristic ( k thresh k_{\text{thresh}} ) described in § 4.3 , the implementation adds visit limits for robustness:
•
Max Visits : Each node may be evaluated at most k max k_{\text{max}} times (default: 5), regardless of belief stability.
•
Cooldown : Re-evaluation requires at least k cool k_{\text{cool}} other evaluations since last visit (default: 2), preventing rapid re-activation loops.
Together with damping, these bound total inference to O ⁡ ( min ⁡ ( k thresh , k max ) ⋅ | V S | ) O(\min(k_{\text{thresh}},k_{\text{max}})\cdot|V_{S}|) .
B.4 Checkpointing
The implementation supports fault-tolerant checkpointing at quiescent points between event processing. Checkpoints capture node beliefs, inbox contents, pending events, and the explanatory graph ( V S , E S ) (V_{S},E_{S}) , enabling recovery without restarting the investigation.
B.5 Initialization Prompts
The investigation begins with a multi-phase initialization that acquires bounded context and selects initial candidates.
B.5.1 Investigation Window Selection
The first step determines the temporal scope by identifying “golden signal” alerts.
select_investigation_window
You are an SRE agent. Your goal is to choose an investigation time window [start_time, end_time] that best captures the onset and peak of the incident, using golden signal alerts as anchors.
Golden signals include alerts indicating: Errors (request error rate, 5xx), Latency (p95/p99), Traffic (throughput drop, no requests).
Ignore noisy platform alerts (watchdog, inhibitors) unless they directly explain golden-signal symptoms.
Input: Alert Summary (JSON with names, entities, timestamps, severity), Application Architecture (service dependencies).
Output: JSON with start_time, end_time, anchor_alerts, golden_signal_alerts, reasoning.
Rules: Prefer application services over infrastructure alerts. start_time ≤ \leq end_time. Use timestamps from alert summary.
B.5.2 Event Filtering
Kubernetes clusters generate thousands of events per hour. We filter events in pages, selecting those relevant to the investigation.
filter_events
You are filtering Kubernetes events to identify those relevant to an ongoing incident investigation.
Relevance Criteria --- INCLUDE:

Warning/Error type events
•
Events on alerting entities or their dependencies
•
Pod lifecycle failures (CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, Evicted)
•

With filtered events and spec changes, the bootstrap prompt selects initial investigation candidates.
bootstrap

Strategy (Golden Signal Priority):
1.

2.

B.6 Abductive Policy Prompt
The explore prompt implements local inference, reasoning over both local evidence and neighbor messages.
explore (Abductive Policy π abd \pi_{\text{abd}} )
You are an SRE support engineer doing RCA using the EoG algorithm.

1.
‘‘What Changed’’ Discipline: A node cannot be Origin if nothing changed within it
2.

3.

4.

Evidence required for every decision (cite logs/events/metrics/traces)
•

•

B.7 Finalize Prompt
When the event queue empties or budget exhausts, the finalize prompt synthesizes findings.
finalize
Summarize the investigation, identifying Root Causes (Frontier) and Causal Graph ( G S G_{S} ). If no frontier found, make the most educated guess given all evidence.
Critical Distinction:
•
Root Cause (contributing_factor: true) = Entity that CAUSED the problem: config changes, deployments, infrastructure failures, fault injections, traffic pattern changes
•
Symptom (contributing_factor: false) = Entity that EXHIBITED the problem: elevated error rates, failures due to upstream causes
Validation Checkpoint: For each contributing_factor: true entity, answer: (1) What specifically changed? (2) When did it change? (3) How does this change explain the symptoms? If you cannot answer all three, it’s likely a symptom.

•
True (Irreducible): Origin in Frontier with no incoming causal edge from another Origin
•
False (Derived): Symptom affected by propagation; failure explained by upstream

B.8 Implementation Notes
The system comprises approximately 3,500 lines of Rust with prompts maintained as Handlebars templates. Key implementation choices:
•
Temperature Zero: All LLM calls use temperature 0 for determinism.
•
Structured Output: All prompts request JSON validated against schemas. Invalid responses trigger a single retry with error correction.
•
Token Budgeting: The Context Contract implements token-aware pagination. When filtered events/changes exceed budgets, tournament-style reduction selects the most relevant items.
•
Entity Normalization: All prompts mandate namespace/Kind/name format for consistent deduplication and graph construction.
The implementation is available as part of the open-source Codex project OpenAI (2025) .

C.2 Judge System Prompt
The LAAJ system prompt defines the evaluation protocol:
LAAJ System Prompt
You are an expert AI evaluator specializing in Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for complex software systems. Your role is to act as a fair, consistent, and precise judge when evaluating RCA model outputs.
You will be provided with:
1.
A Ground Truth (GT) JSON object: true root cause(s), failure propagation path(s), and entity definitions.
2.
A Generated Response JSON object: output from an RCA model to evaluate.
Phase 1: Normalization and Entity Mapping
Before any scoring, normalize and map entities from Generated Response to Ground Truth based on explicit evidence from entity metadata. Do not infer mappings based on position in propagation chain.
Definition of a Confident Match:
A Generated Response entity is a confident match ONLY IF its name field clearly corresponds to the filter and kind of the GT entity.
Entity Name Format:
Generated Response entities use format: namespace/Kind/name
Examples: otel-demo/Deployment/flagd, otel-demo/Service/frontend
CRITICAL - Alias Handling:
If a predicted entity matches an ALIAS of a root cause entity, it MUST be counted as correct. The GT.aliases field contains arrays of equivalent entity IDs. If ANY entity in an alias group has root_cause: true, then matching ANY entity in that alias group counts as correctly identifying the root cause.
Example: Model entity otel-demo/Service/adservice matches GT entity ad-service-1 with filter [".*adservice\\b"].
C.3 Evaluation Metrics
The LAAJ framework evaluates two primary metrics:
•
Root Cause Entity (Precision, Recall, F1): Match contributing_factor=true entities against GT root causes with alias support.
•
Root Cause Reasoning (Average): Semantic similarity of condition descriptions using 0/0.5/1 scoring.
C.3.1 Root Cause Entity Identification
Root Cause Entity Scoring
Method:
1.
Extract all entities with root_cause: true in GT.groups.
2.
Handle Aliases: Check GT.aliases for any alias groups containing a root cause entity. ALL entities in such groups are valid root cause matches.
3.
Extract all entities with contributing_factor: true from Generated Response, preserving order.
4.
Normalize entities to compare against GT root causes.
5.
For EACH predicted entity (in order), determine if it matches any GT root cause entity OR any alias.
6.
Output per-entity match list showing which predicted entities matched GT entities.
7.
Calculate Recall = Correct / Total GT (count each alias group only once).
8.
Calculate Precision = Correct / Total Predicted.
9.
Calculate F1 = (2 × \times Recall × \times Precision) / (Recall + Precision).
Output: List of GT entities, ordered list of predicted entities with per-entity match boolean, Precision, Recall, and F1.
C.3.2 Root Cause Reasoning Accuracy
Root Cause Reasoning Scoring
Method:
1.
Extract the condition of every correct root cause entity from Generated Response.
2.
Extract the condition of corresponding entities from GT.
3.
For each correct root cause entity, compare conditions:
•
Score 1.0: Model’s reason is semantically equivalent to GT’s condition
•
Score 0.5: Model’s condition describes similar resource/action but at least one key detail is missing or imprecise (e.g., GT=‘‘configmap Y featureflag X set’’, Model=‘‘configmap updated’’)
•
Score 0.0: Incorrect or absent model condition
4.
Calculate average of all entity reasoning scores.
5.
If no root cause entity correctly identified, score = 0.
Output: Average reasoning score.
